records.name: Zigrīda
records.facts_used: The dictionary material connects Zigrīda with the Sigrīda family, but its derivation remains unverified. It offers Old Norse sigr, victory, with rīdan, to ride, or a comparison with Sigridh and beauty. The Norwegian Sigrid explanation alone does not settle the history of this exact Latvian form.
records.reason: Research pass completed; unresolved origin remains in backlog.

records.next_steps: Inspect original entries and historical renderings to establish this exact form’s bridge and resolve the two competing root analyses.

records.name: Zigfrīda
records.facts_used: The dictionary places Zigfrīda under Zigfrīds, which refers to Sigfrīds. This family’s account gives Old High German sigu, victory, and fridu, protection or peace. The dictionary establishes the connection without describing the precise mechanism that formed the feminine name. The Zigfrīda entry dates usage to 1922 and a calendar record to 1964. These are two different milestones for this spelling. Neither automatically applies to short-i Zigfrida, whose correspondence still needs verification.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Siliņš pp337/289; explicit cross-reference, not a stated derivational mechanism. Sigfrīds catalogue URL404; exact Zigfrīda/Zigfrīds pages retain the chain.

records.name: Sigruna
records.facts_used: The dictionary explains Sigruna through Old High German sigu, victory, and rūna, magic or mystery. Norwegian Sigrun is explained through Old Norse Sig-rún, victory and secret knowledge. These are linguistic accounts of the family rather than promises about a bearer’s powers. The catalogue gives a Sigruna usage record in 1970. The Language Agency also directly renders Norwegian Sigrun as Sigruna, citing page 227 of the 2003 manual. This record preserves short u and does not establish the separate spelling Sigrūna.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Exact LVA export visually checked;1970 own usage,2003 cited rendering manual. Do not reuse SNL’s1856 Walküre date as a premiere date.

records.name: Ziga
records.facts_used: The dictionary lists Ziga as an affectionate form under several names: Zigfrīda, Zigismunds and Zigmārs. Their explanations share Old High German sigu, victory. It thus records several shortening routes rather than one compulsory full name behind every Ziga. For one related full form, Zigfrīda, the dictionary gives usage in 1922 and a calendar record in 1964. This is a concrete episode in the related form’s history. Those years are not Ziga’s first registration and do not determine which base name a particular family chose.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Multiple explicitly documented diminutive bases share sigu; no unique full-name route selected.1922/1964 belong only to related Zigfrīda, not Ziga.

records.name: Doviltas
records.facts_used: Doviltas is a Lithuanian two-stem name. The guide connects do- with dotas or dovis, in the sphere of gifts and giving, and vilt- with viltis, hope. These element glosses need not be joined into one compulsory literal translation of the entire name. The 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar gives Doviltas with short form Dovas on 23 November. Salys reprinted the list in 1983. This directly records their relationship rather than dating the name’s invention to the reprint; another part of that calendar also lists the name in June.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: PDF317/printed302 exactNovember23 Doviltas(Dovas);PDF309/printed294 June19 also checked. Do not change supplied project dates.

records.name: Felicita
records.facts_used: The Lithuanian guide connects Felicita with Latin felicitas, happiness or good fortune. It belongs to a wider Latin name family whose forms in different languages retain that favourable meaning. The explanation is not a prediction of any particular woman’s good luck. The related form Felicitas illustrates the family’s calendar history: the 1964 list reprinted by Salys in 1983 places it on 23 November, with Felis in parentheses. The source specifically has Felicitas. This does not establish the first use of Felicita without final s.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Exact Lithuanian guide origin; related Felicitas calendar episode explicitly scoped, no sex or exact-form date transferred. GuideNovember20 and curatedMarch7 differ from projectNovember23.

records.name: Klemensas
records.facts_used: Klemensas rests on Latin clemens, merciful or gentle. Salys connects the Lithuanian church form with Polish Klemens and distinguishes earlier Klementas, Klimentas and Klimantas. Alongside the Latin basis, different intermediary languages therefore matter in this family’s history. Salys’s article, reprinted in volume two in 1983, gives Pope Klemensas XIV as a historical example, with his pontificate in 1769–1774. This is the Lithuanian naming of a specific historical person. The pope’s biography is not the name’s first registration in Lithuania.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: PDF109/printed94 visually checked;PDF110/printed95 text distinguishes routes/forms. Avoid presenting legendary martyr details as independently established biography.

The historical date remains source evidence rather than a reason to change this calendar’s day.

records.name: Liubartė
records.facts_used: Liubartė is a Lithuanian two-stem feminine name. The guide connects liu- with liautis, to cease, and bart- with bartis, to fight or quarrel. Pakerys explicitly lists Liubartė alongside Liubartas among -bart- names. The elements do not need an invented life-mission translation. Salys’s reprint of the 1964 calendar places Liubartė on 23 November with short form Barta. Pakerys also examines the exact feminine form in his 2011 accentuation study. These are two concrete examples of written tradition rather than dates when the name was invented.

records.name: Leemet
records.facts_used: Leemet is an Estonian adaptation of Latin Clemens, explicitly identified in both the Estonian dictionary entry and Marja Kallasmaa’s study. Latin clemens means gentle or merciful. Resemblance to local Lemb- names therefore does not itself establish a different root. Mägiste’s 1929 masculine list directly compares Leemet with Clemet, Clement and Kleement. The municipal newspaper Leole also connects Leemet and Leemo with Clemens in November 2005. These printed examples document the name family rather than any child’s first registration.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: MägistePDF36/printed34 exact Leemet, not OCR Leenat. Kallasmaa2017 adaptation explicit; old Lemb-name replacement theory remains qualified and is not asserted here.

records.name: Leemo
records.facts_used: Leole’s name column explicitly connects Leemo with Latin Clemens alongside Leemet and Kleement, glossing clemens as gentle or merciful.
